title: Where people live and how places connect to jobs shape welfare disparities beyond national averages
source_unit: World Bank, People, Jobs, And Places: A Spatial Analysis Of Welfare Disparities In Low- And Middle-Income Countries, and GeoE3 spatial-jobs evidence
geography: Low- and middle-income countries, cities, rural and urban places, neighborhoods, labor markets, and spatial opportunity systems

observations.period: 2026; spatial welfare and jobs analytical frame

denominator.unit: low- and middle-income country spatial welfare and labor-market systems covered by World Bank analysis

spatial_disparity_set.value: income, welfare, labor-market, industry, infrastructure, transport, safety, and location conditions

national_average_boundary.value: country-level averages can conceal persistent differences between places and neighborhoods

observations.method: World Bank spatial analysis using harmonized welfare, labor, industry, geographic, and place-based data for low- and middle-income countries.
observations.uncertainty: Spatial association does not establish that location alone caused welfare or employment outcomes; data resolution, boundary choices, sorting, migration, and unobserved local institutions matter.
observations.subgroup: Urban and rural residents, low-income neighborhoods, workers, firms, commuters, migrants, women, people exposed to hazards, and places with different infrastructure and service access.
observations.counterinterpretation: People and firms can move, adapt, commute, use digital access, or benefit from targeted investment; spatial disadvantage is persistent in some settings but not immovable.

denominator.unit: local employment opportunity systems analyzed through World Bank GeoE3 spatial methods

location_constraint.value: where people live and surrounding conditions influence access to jobs and economic opportunities

constraint_set.value: infrastructure, transport, safety, exposure to natural hazards, and location

policy_use.value: combining labor-market and geographic information enables location-specific employment interventions

observations.method: World Bank GeoE3 framework combining labor-market information with geospatial conditions to identify spatial barriers and opportunity differences.
observations.uncertainty: Geospatial indicators identify exposure and access patterns but do not by themselves estimate worker preferences, employer hiring decisions, commuting costs, or causal employment effects.
observations.subgroup: Job seekers, workers, firms, commuters, women, people in unsafe or hazard-exposed places, transport users, and local employment intermediaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Spatial access can improve through transit, safety, digital connectivity, employer relocation, flexible work, skills, or migration; not every local constraint requires moving jobs or people.

observations.period: 2026; spatial opportunity, welfare, and mobility trade-offs

denominator.unit: people and places in low- and middle-income labor and welfare systems

welfare_pathway.value: place conditions affect access to jobs, services, markets, safety, and economic opportunity

mobility_route.value: migration and commuting can connect people to opportunity but are constrained by housing, transport, information, safety, and local institutions

localization_need.value: employment interventions should be targeted to local constraints rather than treating labor markets as spatially uniform

observations.method: World Bank synthesis connecting spatial welfare disparities, job accessibility, infrastructure, transport, safety, labor markets, and place-sensitive policy.
observations.uncertainty: A place-sensitive framework does not determine whether mobility, local investment, service expansion, or labor-market reform is the best response in a particular location.
observations.subgroup: Residents of lagging places, commuters, migrants, firms, local governments, infrastructure users, and households balancing rent, travel time, safety, and work access.
observations.counterinterpretation: National and regional policies can still matter substantially; local targeting should complement rather than replace macroeconomic, social-protection, education, and labor-market policy.

observations.period: 2026; evidence and governance capacity for spatial inequality

denominator.unit: World Bank spatial-data and employment-policy evidence system

data_integration.value: labor-market data can be combined with geographic information to reveal location-specific constraints

unobserved_risk.value: traditional labor-market analyses can miss infrastructure, transport, safety, hazard, and neighborhood barriers

governance_endpoint.value: better spatial evidence can support more targeted employment, infrastructure, transport, and service decisions

observations.method: World Bank spatial-data, welfare, and jobs evidence synthesis emphasizing geospatial integration and place-sensitive decision-making.
observations.uncertainty: Better spatial measurement does not guarantee fair allocation or improved outcomes; data privacy, coverage, administrative capacity, and political incentives shape implementation.
observations.subgroup: Statistical agencies, planners, local governments, workers, firms, civil society, researchers, and residents represented or missed by spatial data systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fine-grained data can improve targeting but can also stigmatize neighborhoods or enable surveillance; governance should pair spatial precision with rights, transparency, and resident voice.

related_sources.claim: Official reproducibility package for People, Jobs, And Places: A Spatial Analysis Of Welfare Disparities In Low- And Middle-Income Countries.
World Bank GeoE3 evidence and spatial-jobs framework for infrastructure, transport, safety, hazards, and employment access.
World Bank Global Jobs Challenge provides complementary demographic and job-creation context.

boundary: This record adds a spatial opportunity route linking place, transport, infrastructure, safety, hazards, job access, welfare, mobility, data, and local policy. It is not a city-specific commuting estimate, a household location panel, a causal place-effect study, or respondent-level microdata analysis.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank People, Jobs, And Places reproducibility metadata, GeoE3 spatial-jobs publication, and related jobs context were reviewed; spatial-disparity, job-access, constraint, mobility, measurement, and policy claims were cross-checked.
